title: Recursion, Recurrences and the Master Theorem
oneLiner: How to get a Big O out of a function that calls itself: count the call tree, sum it level by level, or read it off the Master theorem.
keyTakeaway: Recursive time is (number of calls) × (work per call). Draw the call tree: its branching factor and depth give the call count, and summing the work level by level gives the total. Recursive space is the depth of that tree times the memory per frame, because only one root to leaf path is ever on the stack at once.
explanation:
A loop tells you its trip count in its header. A recursive function hides it, so you write it down as a recurrence: T(n) is the cost on input size n, expressed through the cost of the calls it makes. Merge sort makes two calls on halves and merges in linear time, so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). Naive Fibonacci makes two calls on n minus 1 and n minus 2, so T(n) = T(n minus 1) + T(n minus 2) + O(1). Writing that line is the first thing to do out loud in an interview.

Then solve it by drawing the call tree. Two numbers do most of the work: the branching factor (calls per call) and the depth (how many times the argument can shrink before hitting the base case). If the argument shrinks by subtraction, the depth is about n; if it shrinks by division, the depth is about log n. Two branches with depth n means about 2ⁿ calls. Two branches with depth log n means 2 to the log n, which is just n. That one contrast explains why halving and branching twice is cheap and subtracting one and branching twice is exponential.

When the work per call is not constant, use the recursion tree method: add the work at each level, then add the levels. For merge sort each level sums to n and there are log n levels, so O(n log n). For T(n) = T(n minus 1) + O(n), the levels are n, n minus 1, n minus 2 and so on, so O(n²).

For divide and conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = a T(n / b) + O(n^d), the Master theorem compares log_b a (how fast the number of calls grows) with d (how fast the work per call shrinks). If log_b a is bigger, the leaves win and the answer is n to the log_b a. If they are equal, every level costs the same and you get n^d log n. If d is bigger, the top call wins and the answer is n^d. It does not cover recurrences that subtract (n minus 1); unroll those.

Memoization changes the count, not the method: with a cache, each distinct argument is computed once, so time becomes (number of distinct states) × (work per state). Fibonacci has n + 1 distinct arguments, so the 2ⁿ tree collapses to O(n). Space is the cache plus the deepest chain of calls still waiting.
